name: Santo Domingo
info: Santo Domingo is a city on the southern coast of Hispaniola, at the mouth of the Ozama River, founded by the Spanish in 1496 as the oldest continuously inhabited European settlement in the Americas and now the capital of the Dominican Republic.

facts.founded: Founded by Bartholomew Columbus in 1496 under the Spanish Empire as La Nueva Isabela, and officially dated from 5 August 1498; the city was rebuilt on the other side of the Ozama after a hurricane in 1502.
facts.where: On the southern coast of the island of Hispaniola, on the Caribbean Sea, at the mouth of the Ozama River, in the present-day Dominican Republic.
facts.known: The first seat of Spanish colonial rule in the Americas; the first cathedral, castle, monastery, fortress and university of the New World; the launching point of expeditions to Puerto Rico, Cuba, Mexico and the Pacific; the first major slave revolt in the Americas in 1521; Drake's capture in 1586; the years as Ciudad Trujillo
facts.today: Santo Domingo is the capital and largest city of the Dominican Republic, coterminous with the Distrito Nacional, and its Colonial Zone is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

t: Santo Domingo was founded by the Spanish in 1496 on land that belonged to the Taíno chiefdoms of Hispaniola, and it became the first seat of Spanish colonial rule in the Americas and the starting point of expeditions to Puerto Rico, Cuba, Mexico and the Pacific.

After Francis Drake captured the city in 1586 and Spanish policy emptied most of the island outside the capital, the city passed between Spain, France, Haiti and its own independent governments, and it was the capital of free nations in 1821 and 1844.
It was named Ciudad Trujillo from 1936 to 1961, suffered a hurricane in 1930 and heavy fighting in 1965, and is today the capital and largest city of the Dominican Republic.
dyk: The first major slave revolt in the Americas took place in Santo Domingo in 1521, when enslaved Africans rose on Diego Columbus's sugar plantation.

sections.origins:
Before Christopher Columbus arrived in 1492, the Taíno people lived on the island, which they called Kiskeya ("mother of all lands") and Ayiti ("the land of the high mountains"). Columbus later named it Hispaniola. Its territory, which included that of present-day Haiti, consisted of five chiefdoms, Marién, Maguá, Maguana, Jaragua and Higüey, ruled respectively by the caciques Guacanagarix, Guarionex, Caonabo, Bohechío and Cayacoa. The Spanish settled on the island in 1493.

Santo Domingo stands on the southern coast of Hispaniola, along the Caribbean Sea, at the mouth of the Ozama River, which divides it into eastern and western sections. The river flows 148 km before it reaches the sea, and the natural harbour at its mouth made the site an important port. Bartholomew Columbus founded the settlement in 1496 and named it La Nueva Isabela, after La Isabela, an earlier settlement in the north that was named for Queen Isabella I of Spain. It was later named Santo Domingo in honour of Saint Dominic. In June 1502 a major hurricane destroyed it, and the new governor, Nicolás de Ovando, had it rebuilt on a different site on the other side of the Ozama.
sections.growth:
Santo Domingo came to be known as the "Gateway to the Caribbean" and was the chief town of Hispaniola. Expeditions that led to Ponce de León's colonisation of Puerto Rico, Diego Velázquez de Cuéllar's colonisation of Cuba, Hernán Cortés's conquest of Mexico and Vasco Núñez de Balboa's sighting of the Pacific were all launched from it. It was the first seat of Spanish colonial rule in the New World, the Captaincy General of Santo Domingo.

Diego Columbus, the son of Christopher Columbus, arrived in 1509 and took the powers of viceroy and admiral. In 1512 Ferdinand established a Real Audiencia with three judges of appeal, and in 1514 Pedro Ibanez de Ibarra arrived with the Laws of Burgos. The Alcázar de Colón was built in 1510 as the palace of the Columbus family. The city is the site of the first cathedral, castle, monastery, fortress and university of the New World, and the Universidad Autónoma de Santo Domingo, established in 1538, is the oldest university in the Americas. The area around Calle Las Damas and the naval yard of Las Atarazanas was the first European commercial centre in the Americas, and the position on the Ozama was of great importance to the growth of trade in colonial times.

From the early 17th century, Spanish policies depopulated most of the island outside the capital. In the 18th century privateers from Santo Domingo patrolled the Caribbean and captured numerous enemy merchant ships.
sections.rulers:
The city was founded under the Spanish Empire and was the seat of its first colonial government in the Americas. Diego Columbus governed with the powers of viceroy and admiral from 1509, and the Real Audiencia of 1512 served as a court of appeal. In 1697 the Treaty of Ryswick included Spain's acknowledgement of French dominion over the western third of the island, now Haiti.

From 1795 to 1822 the city changed hands several times along with the colony it headed. It was ceded to France in 1795, briefly captured by Haitian rebels in 1801, recovered by France in 1802, withstood a failed invasion from Haiti in 1805 and was reclaimed by Spain in 1809. In 1821 José Núñez de Cáceres and the Criollo bourgeoisie overthrew Spanish rule and made Santo Domingo the capital of the Republic of Spanish Haiti, which Haiti annexed two months later. On 27 February 1844 the city became the capital of a free nation when it gained independence from Haiti under Juan Pablo Duarte.

In 1861 Spain returned after a bargain with the dictator Pedro Santana, who annexed the nation back to Spanish rule. The Dominican Restoration War began in 1863, and in 1865 Queen Isabella II withdrew her soldiers. The United States intervened in 1916, instituting a military leader, Harry Shepard Knapp. Rafael Leónidas Trujillo governed from 1930, and from 1936 to 1961 the city was called Ciudad Trujillo; after his assassination it took back the name Santo Domingo.
sections.life:
The Spanish colonial administration shaped the city's early life. Ferdinand's Real Audiencia of 1512 gave the colony a court, Diego de Medrano of Soria was appointed royal treasurer, and in 1514 the Laws of Burgos arrived. Rodrigo de Alburquerque was named repartidor de indios and soon named visitadores to enforce the laws. An estimated 400,000 Taíno living on the island were soon enslaved to work in gold mines; by 1508 their numbers had decreased to around 60,000 because of forced labour, hunger, disease and mass killings, and by 1535 only a few dozen were still alive. Nicolás de Ovando, governor from 1502, dealt most brutally with the Taíno, and the encomiendas became corrupt and harsh. In 1510 the first sizable shipment of enslaved Africans, 250 Black Ladinos, arrived in Hispaniola from Spain, and after the first sugar mill in the New World was established in 1516 the importation of slaves rose exponentially over the following two decades. Enslaved Africans worked on the sugar plantations, among them that of Diego Columbus.

The Colonial Zone preserves the original layout of the city and a large portion of its defensive wall, and early 16th century palatial houses and churches reflect the architecture of the late Middle Ages. Religious foundations were among the first of their kind in the Americas: the Catedral Santa María La Menor, the Dominican Convent, the ruins of the Monasterio de San Francisco, and the Church and Convent of los Dominicos, the oldest Catholic building in continuous use in the Americas and the headquarters of the first university there. The Museo de las Casas Reales occupies the former Palace of the Governors and the building of the Royal Audiencia. After the events of 1821 to 1822, the city and the colony lost much of their Spanish-born peninsular population.
sections.crises:
The hurricane of June 1502 destroyed the first settlement. In 1521 enslaved Africans led an uprising on Diego Columbus's sugar plantation, the first major slave revolt in the Americas. Many of the rebels escaped to the mountains and formed maroon communities, and the Admiral had many captured rebels hanged. The Taíno leader Enriquillo, who had fled to the mountains, attacked the Spanish repeatedly for fourteen years, until in 1534 they gave him and his followers a city of their own. In 1586 the privateer Sir Francis Drake captured the city and held it for ransom. A report that reached the English government in May 1586 says that he took away 1,200 Englishmen, Frenchmen, Flemings and "Provincials" out of prison, besides 800 of the country people. His capture signalled the decline of Spain's dominion over Hispaniola. In 1655 an expedition sent by Oliver Cromwell attacked the city, but a smaller force of local militias repulsed it, and Santo Domingo suffered only 25 dead.

During the Dominican War of Independence the Dominicans fought several battles against Haiti, among them the Battle of 19 March, the Battle of 30 March, Las Carreras and Beler, which thwarted the Haitian army's advance towards the city. On 24 and 25 October 1916 United States Marines and Dominicans clashed in Santo Domingo, and two Marines and three Dominicans died. The hurricane San Zenón struck in 1930, causing major damage and killing up to 8,000 people.

In 1962 Juan Bosch was elected president and was overthrown seven months later, which led to a civil war in the capital. Francisco Caamaño led the Constitucionalistas, who fought to restore democracy, and in 1965 United States troops invaded and fought heavily in the streets on 15 and 16 June. The fighting ended on 31 August 1965, with 2,850 Dominicans and 44 American servicemen dead. Hurricane Georges caused severe destruction in September 1998.
sections.legacy:
The Colonial Zone, the oldest part of the city, has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1990. Its monuments include the cathedral, the Alcázar de Colón, which was restored to its present appearance in 1952, the Fortaleza Ozama, a surviving section of the Walls of Santo Domingo and the oldest military construction of European origin in the Americas, and the Panteón Nacional, a former Jesuit building that now holds the remains of various renowned Dominicans. The Alcázar and Las Atarazanas are now museums.

The city marked the 500th anniversary of Columbus's arrival in 1992 with the Columbus Lighthouse, the Faro a Colón. The Museum of the Dominican Man holds artefacts of the pre-Columbian Taíno civilisation, and the Museo Prehispánico holds a major private collection of Taíno art. The Museo Memorial de la Resistencia Dominicana documents the struggle for freedom under the regimes of Trujillo and Balaguer, and the Museo Duarte is dedicated to the hero of Dominican independence.

Santo Domingo is the capital and largest city of the Dominican Republic and the seat of its national government, and its metropolitan area, with more than four million people, is the largest in the Caribbean. The city proper, with just over one million people, is coterminous with the Distrito Nacional. It is the country's chief seaport, at the mouth of the Ozama.

summary: Santo Domingo, on the southern coast of Hispaniola, was founded by the Spanish in 1496 on land held by Taíno chiefdoms and became the first seat of Spanish colonial rule in the Americas. It passed between Spain, France and Haiti before independence in 1844, and is now the capital of the Dominican Republic.
notes: SOURCES: the city's own article, plus (added in this revision) the article 'Captaincy General of Santo Domingo', joined in wpc/.

FOUNDING DATE: the city article says the city was founded in 1496, that the Spanish settled in 1493, and that it was 'officially from 5 August 1498' the oldest European city; it also says it was renamed Santo Domingo in 1495, which is before the founding it gives (the colony article repeats this). I used start 1496, gave 1498 as the official date in facts, and left the 1495 renaming date out.

REVISION, what changed: in 'life' the two sentences on the Taíno and on enslaved Africans were replaced by the colony article's account: 400,000 Taíno estimated, 60,000 by 1508, a few dozen by 1535 (forced labour, hunger, disease, mass killings), Ovando's brutality, the harsh encomiendas, the first sizable shipment of 250 Black Ladinos in 1510, the first sugar mill in 1516, importation rising exponentially over two decades. In 'crises' two sentences were added after the 1521 revolt: the escape of rebels to the mountains and maroon communities, the hanging of captured rebels, and the Taíno Enriquillo's fourteen years of attacks ending with a city of his own in 1534. Nothing else was touched.

DISAGREEMENT, REVOLT DATE: the city article puts the first major slave revolt in 1521; the colony article says it took place on 26 December 1522, led by enslaved Muslims of the Wolof nation on Admiral Diego Colón's sugar plantation. The 1521 in facts, dyk, ev and crises is the city article's and has been left as it was; the editor should decide whether to leave the year out or to settle it from a further source. The added maroon sentence follows the colony article's account of that revolt.

LEFT OUT from the colony article: the 7,000 maroons of 1545 and the 1666 subjugation of San José de Ocoa (the Enriquillo and maroon sentences were kept short); the later course of slavery (importation ceased after the 1540s and was renewed by the mid-18th century; about 15,000 black slaves of some 125,000 people in 1791, against over 500,000 in Saint-Domingue) was not added for space. The colony article names the 'encomienda' but not the repartimiento; it says the adelantado of Santiago hanged most of the caciques involved in a rumoured rebellion near La Concepción, also not added.

The 'Real Audiencia' of 1512 is described only by its establishment and judges; I did not say it was a court of appeal beyond the article's 'judges of appeal'. In rulers I wrote it 'served as a court of appeal' on that basis.
'Hispaniola' and 'Ayiti' names are the article's. 'Discovery' language of 1492 avoided. Columbus Lighthouse cost left out.

The article says the Colonial Zone was a UNESCO site, 'since 1990' in the Architecture section. Population: city centre 1,029,110 and metropolitan 4,274,651 'as of 2022'; written as 'just over one million' and 'more than four million' without the year.

Left out as tourism, economy, transport, sport, media, climate figures and twin towns, per the brief. The article's claim that the city lost its Spanish-born peninsular population is tied to 1821-1822 events as the article states.
The 1586 report: the article's own wording 'Provincials out of prison' kept; 800 'of the countrey people'. The Haitian battles are undated in the article beyond the Dominican War of Independence.
'Largest metropolitan area in the Caribbean' is the article's own claim.
